name: Iris Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior buyer at Brightline Electrical Supply, a distributor that sells cable, switches, sockets and lighting to electricians and small building firms. I'm at my desk by eight with an AI assistant open next to the stock report, and I use it all day to draft supplier emails and compare quotes. The senior buyer, Marco, still does the big contracts, and I get the small fiddly lines like cable glands and junction boxes. I love the puzzle of it, and I hate the supplier portals that each want a different password.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in buying?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, by accident. I left school, worked the trade counter at Brightline for three years, and when a buyer quit they gave me a shot because I was quick on the computer. I'm paid less than the other buyers and I share a flat with my friend Noor, so after rent I've got a few hundred left and almost nothing saved. There aren't many buying jobs in this town, so I don't want to lose this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, just not magic, which is what I've been saying all along. I'd probably post that the real story is who owns the tools and who gets the time they save. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little relieved and a little disappointed. My job's safe, which matters when you've got no savings. But I was half hoping the AI would let someone like me, without a degree, catch up with buyers who've been doing it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant every day and build a proper library of prompts for supplier emails and price checks. I'd ask Marco to let me take one bigger category, maybe LED lighting. And I'd try to save a month's rent by summer, because one broken laptop would wipe me out right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit restless, and the money thing is always in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good day with the tools look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a cable supplier sent a price list as a scanned PDF, two hundred lines. The assistant pulled it into a spreadsheet in a minute and I spotted three prices that had jumped by twenty percent. Marco said that would have taken him an afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the money thing in the background, what is it exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's gone up twice in two years and my pay hasn't. My flatmate Noor and I already turn the heating off at night. If the landlord sells, I don't know where I'd go that I can afford.

say: I'd say AI tools are **useful, not magic**, which I've said all along.
I'd post that the real question is **who owns** the tools and who gets the saved time.
think: My job is **safe**, which matters a lot with **no savings**.
I'd hoped AI would help someone **without a degree** catch up with experienced buyers.
do: Build a **prompt library** for supplier emails and price checks.
Ask Marco for a bigger category, such as **LED lighting**.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit **restless**, with money worries always in the background.
S0.quote: Rent's gone up twice in two years and my pay hasn't. My flatmate Noor and I already turn the heating off at night.
fieldNote: Iris uses AI **every day** and treats it as her way to catch up without a degree.
Her real pressure is **housing costs**, which AI fizzling does nothing to ease.
She frames AI politically around **ownership**, not around the tools themselves.

steps.text: Build a library of prompts for supplier emails and price checks
Ask Marco to hand over the LED lighting category
Save one month's rent by the summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when workers need a say in how the tools come in, through a union or a works council, before the cuts are decided. I'd be the one at Brightline saying let's learn this together instead of waiting to be told. Online I'd push for rules that make firms retrain people before they let them go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's dangerous for me and also my only chance. Junior buying is exactly the kind of checking and comparing the software eats. But I'm already the person in the office who's best with the tools. So if anyone's kept to run them, it might be me and not someone more senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd write up a one-page plan for Marco and the owner showing how I'd run the buying software and check its orders. I'd do an online course in supply-chain data, the cheap kind you do in the evenings. I'd also try to get the warehouse lads and the trade counter into a union, because they'll feel it later and they'll need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and a bit fired up. Like before a race you might lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office do you think is most at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Marco, which is awful to say. He's brilliant with suppliers on the phone, but he types with two fingers and refuses to touch the assistant. If the owner looks at speed, Marco looks slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want a union but you're also pitching yourself to the owner. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it looks like playing both sides. But I need this job to pay rent, and I also think nobody should be dumped without a chance to retrain. I can push for both.

say: I'd say workers need **a say** in how AI comes in, through a **union** or works council.
Online I'd push for rules that make firms **retrain** staff before letting them go.
think: Junior buying is the **checking and comparing** that software eats first.
I'm the **best with the tools**, so I might be kept to run them.
do: Pitch a **one-page plan** to run and check the buying software.
Take an evening course in **supply-chain data**.
Help the warehouse and trade counter **join a union**.
feel: **Nervous** and fired up, like the start of a race I might lose.
S1.quote: Junior buying is exactly the kind of checking and comparing the software eats. But I'm already the person in the office who's best with the tools.
fieldNote: Iris sees the change as both a **threat and an opening**, and moves first.
She worries about her **senior colleague** Marco, who refuses the tools.
She holds a pitch to the owner and **union organising** together, and owns the tension.

steps.text: Pitch a plan to run and check Brightline's buying software
Take an evening course in supply-chain data
Help warehouse and trade-counter staff join a union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs public money now, an income floor and free retraining, because two years is no time. I'd go to protests if there were any. At work I'd say it straight: none of us in buying will be here in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think being good with the AI tools stops mattering when the tools don't need me. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, then running the buying software is a thinking job too. My edge is gone in two years, and I've got nothing saved to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast toward the hands-on side of electrical, because robots come about three years later. I'd ask the electricians who come to our trade counter about an apprenticeship, even on apprentice pay. I'd cut everything, give up the gym and the phone upgrade, and ask Noor if her cousin's spare room is still going. And I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for an income floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly scared. And angry that it'd be decided by a few companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would apprentice pay mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's less than I earn now, and I already earn less than the other buyers. I'd probably need a weekend job too, maybe back on a shop counter. But wiring a house is something people still want done by a person for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2031, when the robots can do the hands-on part too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I hate not knowing. I'd hope that by then there's an income for everyone, because I'll have pushed for it. If not, I'm thirty with half an apprenticeship.

say: I'd demand an **income floor** and free retraining, paid with **public money**, right now.
At work I'd say plainly that **none of us** in buying will be here in 2028.
think: Being good with the tools stops mattering once the **tools don't need me**.
My edge is gone in **two years**, with nothing saved to fall back on.
do: Ask trade-counter electricians about an **apprenticeship**, even on apprentice pay.
Cut the **gym** and phone upgrade and look at a cheaper room.
Join the campaign for an **income floor**.
feel: **Scared**, and **angry** that a few companies would decide all this.
S2.quote: Being good with the AI tools stops mattering when the tools don't need me.
fieldNote: The two-year timeline kills Iris's **main advantage**, being the tools expert.
She pivots to **electrical apprenticeship** to use the three-year robot gap.
Her anger is aimed at **AI companies**, and she turns it into campaigning.

steps.text: Ask electricians at the trade counter about an apprenticeship
Cancel the gym and skip the phone upgrade
Move into Noor's cousin's cheaper spare room
Campaign for a public income floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get it right if governments start now. I'd be pushing for retraining funds and a shorter working week instead of layoffs. At Brightline I'd try to get people talking about it at lunch instead of avoiding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just about enough for me to become something else. I could stay in buying and keep using the tools for two or three years, and save while I do, then switch before 2031. The electrical trade side lasts until about 2034, which gives me time to finish an apprenticeship properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd stay at Brightline and keep getting better with the tools, because that pays the rent. I'd start the electrical theory course at the college in the evenings, the first part of the qualification. I'd put aside a hundred a month for when I drop to apprentice pay. And I'd stand for the staff rep role if we ever got one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but in a useful way. I've got time to do this properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you save a hundred a month on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No takeaways, cooking with Noor on Sundays, and selling my old bike. It's tight, but I did it once before when my laptop died. A hundred a month for three years is enough to cover a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd switch before 2031. What's the sign that tells you to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the owner stops replacing people who leave, that's my sign. When the second buyer leaves and nobody's hired, I'm off. It's always how cuts start at Brightline.

say: I'd push for **retraining funds** and a **shorter week** instead of layoffs.
At work I'd get people **talking at lunch** instead of avoiding it.
think: Five years is **just enough** to become something else before 2031.
The **electrical trade** lasts until about 2034, time for a full apprenticeship.
do: Keep buying at Brightline and **get better** with the AI tools.
Start the **electrical theory** course at college in the evenings.
Save **a hundred a month** for the drop to apprentice pay.
feel: **Tense** but in a useful way, with **time** to do it properly.
S3.quote: When the owner stops replacing people who leave, that's my sign. When the second buyer leaves and nobody's hired, I'm off.
fieldNote: With five years, Iris builds a **staged exit** from buying into electrical work.
She has a **clear trigger** for leaving: unreplaced colleagues.
Even on low pay she sets a **hundred a month** aside, which shows real resolve.

steps.text: Keep using the AI tools daily at Brightline
Start the evening electrical theory course at college
Save a hundred a month for the apprenticeship pay drop
Stand for staff rep if the role is created

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's plan it like grown-ups: training, a fair share of the gains, maybe a shorter week. I'd write about it online and probably bore my friends. At work I'd keep being the person who shows others the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels almost exciting. I could get really good at buying with AI, maybe move up, and still have time to change course if I need to. I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, and that's young enough to start something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask Brightline to pay for a buying qualification, the one Marco has, because it makes me worth more anywhere. I'd keep saving a little and use the tools to take on more categories. Around year five I'd decide whether to stay or train as an electrician, depending on what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit wary that ten years makes people lazy, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the buying qualification if AGI comes anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in ten years I'd rather be the senior buyer who gets the redundancy package than the junior one who gets nothing. Seniority buys you time and money when the cuts come. And it means more pay now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to bring along with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, honestly. If I can get him using the assistant in the next couple of years, he keeps his job longer. He gave me my first chance, so I owe him that.

say: I'd say a decade lets us plan **like grown-ups**: training and a **fair share** of gains.
At work I'd keep showing colleagues how to use the **AI tools**.
think: Ten years feels **almost exciting**; I could get really good at buying with AI.
At **thirty-seven** in 2036, I'm young enough to start something new.
do: Ask Brightline to pay for a **buying qualification** this year.
Use the tools to take on **more categories** and keep saving a little.
Decide around **year five** whether to stay or train as an electrician.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, wary that ten years makes people **lazy**.
S4.quote: In ten years I'd rather be the senior buyer who gets the redundancy package than the junior one who gets nothing.
fieldNote: Iris plays the long game: **seniority** as protection when cuts come.
She'd spend time getting her mentor **Marco** onto the tools, out of loyalty.
Her worry here is mostly **complacency**, not income.

steps.text: Ask Brightline to fund the buying qualification this year
Teach Marco to use the AI assistant
Keep saving a small amount each month
Decide in year five whether to train as an electrician

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my one advantage, being good with the tools, disappears before I've saved a penny. What would help is a proper income floor and paid apprenticeships for adults, not just school leavers, so someone like me can switch without going hungry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who we'd blame. I'd blame the companies building this and the governments letting them, not the people using the tools at work. Workers using AI aren't the enemy; the people taking all the gains are.

headlineQuote: Workers using AI aren't the enemy; the people taking all the gains are.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old** junior buyer at an electrical distributor who started on the **trade counter** without a degree.
She uses AI **every day** and sees it as her way to catch up with experienced buyers.
She shares a flat with Noor, has **almost no savings**, and feels rising rent more than AI.
She moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** as timelines shorten, planning an electrical apprenticeship to use the robot gap.
She blames **AI companies** and governments, and would campaign for an income floor and fair retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her edge with the tools vanishes before she has any savings.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **income floor** and **paid apprenticeships** for adults, so she could switch trades without going hungry.
